title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems
topic: Probabilistic Methods->Monte Carlo and Sampling Methods
claim: A single scalar knob continuously moves outputs from a blurry mean estimate to faithful multimodal samples, trading distortion for perceptual quality.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared legend on top, titles carry the parameter value
description: A shared legend across the top defines three marker types: black dots for measurements, green dots for ground truth P1, and red dots for PnP output. Below it are three scatter-plot panels in a row. Each panel titled PnP-Flow(D_{s,t}) with a different lookahead t: t=s, t=s+0.27, and t=1. In every panel the black measurements cluster at the left, and the green ground-truth samples form two blobs at the upper and lower right. In the left panel the red points collapse into a diagonal streak between the two modes, which is the posterior mean. In the middle panel the red points concentrate in both modes with a thin bridge between them. In the right panel the red points overlap both green modes. The eye goes first to the red points changing shape from left to right.
caption: PnP with average denoisers on a 2D mixture-of-Gaussians inverse problem (y = Hx + σϵ, with H a rotation+scaling operator and σ = 0.3). Ds,t denotes the average denoiser (defined formally in Section 3.1). The lookahead t controls the DP trade-off: at t = s the denoiser is MMSE and PnP reconstructions concentrate at the posterior mean, which for this symmetric bimodal posterior lies between the two modes, yielding low distortion but poor perceptual quality; as t →1, the lookahead progressively restores the bimodal structure, recovering samples from both modes at the cost of higher distortion; details of this experiment are in Appendix B.4.
abstract: Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA ($128\times 128$) and AFHQ ($256\times 256$) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings.
